subject: Agriculture
title: The First Domesticated Animals
description: A short lesson to help you apply The First Domesticated Animals.

hook.text: Dogs came first—about 15,000 years ago. But the real livestock revolution started with goats and sheep.

buildup.text: Around 10,000 years ago, people in the Near East began keeping wild goats in pens instead of hunting them.

discovery.text: Captive animals provided meat on demand, plus milk, wool, and leather—a living supply chain.

twist.text: Cattle came later and were harder to tame. Wild aurochs stood six feet tall and were dangerously aggressive.

climax.text: Within a few thousand years, livestock spread worldwide. Animals became partners in building civilization.

punchline.text: Farming animals turned hunters into herders.

quiz.question: Which animals were among the first livestock domesticated for farming?

details.summary: The first domesticated animals—dogs, sheep, goats, cattle, and pigs—were tamed thousands of years ago to provide food, fiber, labor, and companionship. This topic covers when and where each species was domesticated and how animal husbandry co-evolved with farming.
details.whyItMatters: Domesticated animals transformed agriculture by providing meat, milk, wool, and draft power. They made farming more productive and enabled humans to exploit landscapes unsuitable for crops.
takeaways: Dogs were the first domesticated animal, some 15,000 years ago from wolves
Sheep and goats were domesticated around 10,000 years ago in the Fertile Crescent
Cattle provided draft power that made plowing heavy soils possible

faq.question: Which animals were domesticated first and where?
faq.answer: Dogs were first, domesticated from wolves around 15,000 years ago. Sheep and goats followed around 10,000 BCE in the Fertile Crescent, then cattle and pigs. Chickens were domesticated in Southeast Asia, and horses on the Central Asian steppe.

faq.question: How did animal domestication change farming?
faq.answer: Animals provided reliable protein from meat, milk, and eggs; fibers from wool; fertilizer from manure; and critical draft power for plowing, transport, and threshing—multiplying what a single farmer could produce and the land they could work.
